title: How to find pi by dropping a needle (and how one man faked it)
description:
Draw lines 3 cm apart and drop a 2.5 cm needle: it lands across a line with chance 5/(3π), about 53 times in 100, so counting crossings gives you π (Buffon's needle). In 1901 Lazzarini reported 3,408 drops and π = 355/113 = 3.1415929, right to six decimals. An honest run of 3,408 drops is typically off by about 0.05; 3,408 = 16 × 213, and 213 drops with 113 crossings gives exactly 355/113, which suggests he stopped when the count fit. Six honest digits would take about 100 trillion drops.

Numbers checked in code: the exact fractions, 1,000,000 simulated needle drops and 100,000 simulated 3,408-drop runs. Source: Wikipedia, Buffon's needle problem.

beats.say: Drop a needle on lined paper, and it tells you pi.
No circle, no ruler. Just a floor, lines and a needle. And one man who got it far too right.
Draw lines 3 centimeters apart. Drop a needle 2.5 centimeters long, again and again, and count how often it lands across a line.
Buffon proved the chance is five over three pi. About 53 in 100. Turn that around, and your count tells you pi.
In 1901, Lazzarini did it 3,408 times and got pi right to six decimals. Suspiciously right.
An honest run that size is usually off by 0.05. That's 3.1.
The giveaway: 3,408 is 16 times 213. And 213 drops with 113 crossings gives 355 over 113, a famous fraction for pi. Looks like he stopped when it fit.
Six honest digits would take about 100 trillion drops.
Drop 100 needles. About how many cross a line?
